ANIMAL CATEGORIES LESSON · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Small Animals — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches four small workers, one wonder at a time.

What is this?

Small animals are the little furred workers of the animal world: mice that squeeze through gaps the size of a coin, guinea pigs that talk in squeaks, moles that dig underground highways, and beavers that build dams bigger than a car.

What does it mean?

Size is not strength: a beaver changes whole rivers, and a mouse survives everywhere on Earth except the poles. Small bodies run on clever plans.

What does the child need to know?

Mice can fit through coin-sized holes; guinea pigs squeak "wheek!" for food and are famous gentle pets; moles are nearly blind and dig with shovel-hands; beaver teeth never stop growing, so the chewing never stops either.

Why this matters

Children love an underdog, and the small-animals card is a whole team of them — biggest engineering from the smallest engineers.

What it teaches

Respect for creatures usually dismissed, size-comparison math (how many mice tall is the fridge?), and cause-and-effect building play.

Words to learn

mousetinyguinea pigwheekmoletunnelbeaverdamlodgegnaw

Say this to your child

“"Small animals, big work! The mouse fits through a coin-sized door, the guinea pig squeaks for snacks, the mole digs its own highways, and the beaver builds a house that changes the whole river!"”

Step by step

  1. The mouse: squeeze test — a mouse flattens its skull to fit through gaps the size of a coin. That is how it gets everywhere.
  2. The guinea pig: the talker — "wheek, wheek!" means food, and popcorning (little jumps) means joy. It is the card’s most famous pet.
  3. The mole: underground digger — shovel-shaped hands, tiny eyes, tunnels with bedrooms and worm pantries.
  4. The beaver: the engineer — it fells trees with its teeth, piles them into dams, and the pond behind the dam becomes a whole new neighborhood for frogs, fish and ducks.
  5. The small rule: small does not mean weak — measure the beaver’s work against the beaver’s size.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the mouse has big round ears, the guinea pig sits plump and calm, the mole holds its pink shovel-hands forward, and the beaver shows its flat paddle tail and orange-gnawing teeth.

Ask your child

"How small a hole can a mouse fit through?" (a coin-sized one) "Which small animal builds dams?" (the beaver) "What does the guinea pig say when it is snack time?" (wheek, wheek!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might try to post a coin through a mouse-sized gap to test the claim, popcorn (jump for joy) exactly like a guinea pig at snack time, or dam a garden puddle with heroic sticks.

Out in the real world

Beaver dams are real road-trip sights across Canada and the northern US — look for the cone of sticks and the new pond behind it. Guinea pigs live in classrooms everywhere and squeak loudest when the fridge opens.

Try it together

Dam builders: pile couch cushions across a doorway and hold back a storm of rolled socks. The wave wins only if the dam leaks — the beaver always has one more stick.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which small animal builds dams?" (the beaver) "What does the mole do all day?" (digs tunnels) "How does the guinea pig ask for food?" (wheek, wheek!)

This lesson pairs with the Small Animals flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animal Categories.
